newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Flatten those core market trades.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Flatten those core market trades.

text.p: Bond yield curves will flatten in U.S., German and British markets over the next few weeks, but will steepen in peripheral Europe, analysts said on Tuesday.

"The two- to 30-year U.S. spread has broken through a key technical level of 76-77 basis points and can get down to 30 basis points," said Steven Major, head of global bond research at Credit Lyonnais in London.
An increase in the federal funds target rate has been priced into June Eurodollar futures, but is not reflected in the shorter end of the U.S. bond yield curve, analysts said.
June Eurodollars were quoted at 94.19 in automated trade at 1140 GMT, implying money market rates of 5.81 percent, against a Fed funds rate of 5.25 percent.
Two-year Treasury notes were yielding 6.08 percent.
"That's a tight spread versus Fed funds and three-month money," said Major.

The two-to 30-year U.S. yield spread has already narrowed from around 90 basis points at the end of January to 74 basis points currently, analysts said, and underperformance at the shorter end will flatten it further.
Investors looking to sell expensively-priced short-dated U.S. paper can find most value in medium dates, they added.
"We would recommend five to 10 years, when the long bond reaches a yield of 6.99 percent or higher," said David Crofts, sales executive for international bonds at Williams de Broe in London.
The yield on the U.S. long bond approached those levels late last week, before February employment data lifted the market. It yielded 6.82 percent at 1152 GMT.
Rate rises are a less immediate concern in Germany, but markets are starting to price in an upward move by the end of 1997 from the current 2.50 percent discount rate, analysts said.
"The short end is under pressure," said Ifty Islam, European bond strategist at Merrill Lynch International in London. Islam recommends selling two-year German bonds, and buying fives.
Major agreed. "The five-year cash is cheap to swaps, and the Bundesbank's issuance burden is shifting towards two years."
In Britain, short sterling is discounting a rise in base rates from their current six percent by June. Britain must hold a general election by May 22 at the latest.
But as in the U.S., short-dated bonds look expensive, analysts said.

"For domestic investors, the yields are rather skinny," said Richard Warburton, director of fixed interest at Williams de Broe. "But the currency has made them extremely popular with Japanese investors."
The strength of sterling has also drawn Japanese money towards short-dated Eurosterling bonds, Warburton said.
Canada's Export Development Corp, New Zealand and the World Bank are among high-profile borrowers to have launched short-dated sterling bonds in recent weeks.
Scope will be limited for the gilt curve to flatten further ahead of the election, analysts said.

But in peripheral Europe, worries about progress towards a single currency are weighing on the longer end of the curve and encouraging a steepening trend, and investors should look to shorter dates, analysts said.
"In Italy and in Spain, I would go for two years," said Major.
Two-year Italian bonds yielded 6.834 percent and two-year Spanish debt yielded 5.627 percent at early afternoon in Europe.
